data.summary:
Input: An integer n representing the number of vertices labeled from 0 to n - 1 and a list of undirected edges.
Output: An integer representing the total number of connected components in the graph.
Rules: Each edge is a pair of vertices. No duplicate edges will appear.

data.key_insight: A connected component is a set of vertices that can reach each other. Initially, each vertex is its own component (n components). Each given edge merges two components. Using Union-Find, we can efficiently perform these merges and keep track of the remaining number of components.

steps.title: Initialize Union-Find Data Structure
steps.detail: Create a parent array where each node is its own parent and set the initial component count to n.

steps.title: Iterate Over Edges
steps.detail: For each edge connecting two nodes, find the roots of their respective components.

steps.title: Union Components
steps.detail: If the two nodes belong to different components, union them by making one root point to the other, and decrement the component count by 1.

steps.title: Return Total Components
steps.detail: After processing all edges, return the final component count.

data.overview: This algorithm uses a Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find) data structure to find the number of connected components in an undirected graph. It starts by treating every node as its own component and decrements the component count whenever an edge successfully merges two previously disjoint components.
data.intuition: Imagine a group of people at a party. Initially, every person is in their own independent circle of one. When two people are introduced via an edge, their respective social circles merge into a single larger circle, reducing the total count of distinct circles by one.

flow_nodes.label: Initialize parent and components
flow_nodes.detail: Set each node as its own parent and components equal to n.

flow_nodes.label: Iterate through edges
flow_nodes.detail: Loop over each edge [u, v] in the edges list.

flow_nodes.label: Union endpoints
flow_nodes.detail: Find the roots of u and v, and merge them if they differ.

flow_nodes.label: Return components
flow_nodes.detail: Return the final count of remaining connected components.

pitfalls: Forgetting to apply path compression in the find function, leading to slow performance.
Not decrementing the component count when two separate sets are successfully merged.
Incorrectly handling graph nodes that have no edges connected to them.

events.label: Coach: pattern, brute force and its bottleneck

data.pattern_summary: Disjoint Set Union (also known as Union-Find) tracks elements partitioned into a number of disjoint sets. Reach for it when you need to group items, merge sets, and efficiently query if two items belong to the same group.

pattern_options.name: Disjoint Set Union
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We need to merge vertices connected by edges and track how many separate components remain.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers applies to sorted linear data structures, not graph connectivity.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Sliding window finds subarrays or substrings of a specific size or condition, not graph components.

pattern_options.name: Greedy
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Graph connectivity is about structural reachability, not making locally optimal choices at each step.

signals.hint: Implies a symmetric relationship between vertices, forming mutual groups.
Indicates we need to count disjoint groups of connected vertices.

data.brute_force_idea: Initialize each vertex as its own component. Iterate through each edge, and for each edge, merge the components of its two vertices. Finally, count the number of unique component roots.
data.brute_force_why: For each of the e edges, we call find() which traverses parent pointers up to n steps in the worst-case skewed tree structure.
data.bottleneck: The find function repeatedly walks up the parent chain to find the root without flattening the structure, leading to redundant traversals.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how the find function navigates the tree of parents.
Notice that every time we look up the root of a vertex, we re-walk the exact same edges to the top.
Consider how you might update the parent pointers during the lookup so future lookups take fewer steps.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The optimized solution uses Disjoint Set Union (DSU) with path compression. Instead of rescanning trees repeatedly from scratch during queries, path compression flattens the tree structure during every find operation so future lookups take nearly constant time.

derivation.note: Allocates the parent array once for all n nodes.
Iterates through each of the E edges once.
Calls union for each edge, which executes find operations bounded by the inverse Ackermann function.

data.time_summary: Initializing the parent array takes O(n) time. Processing all edges in the loop takes O(E * alpha(n)) time, where alpha is the inverse Ackermann function. Combining these gives the total time complexity of O(n + E * alpha(n)).
data.space_summary: The space complexity is O(n) because the parent array stores an integer for each of the n nodes.
data.takeaway: When tracking connected components or equivalence classes that dynamically merge, use Disjoint Set Union with path compression to reduce lookups to nearly constant time.
mistakes: Forgetting to apply path compression in the find function, which degrades tree traversal to linear time.
Failing to decrement the component count when two distinct roots are successfully merged.
Confusing vertex labeling bounds and index ranges when initializing the parent list.
